title: A school for beginners (Prologue)
hookLine: Benedict hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome

cards: A bright sticker on the back of a car: student driver. The cars behind it soften. They give more room.
They don't honk when it stalls at the light. The sticker doesn't make the driver any better. It just tells the truth: this person is learning, so be patient.
Saint Benedict, near the end of the Prologue to his Rule, puts something like that sticker on the whole monastery.

teach.h: A SCHOOL OF THE LORD'S SERVICE.
teach.b: Benedict tells his monks what he's building. In Latin: dominici schola servitii, a school of the Lord's service. Not a fortress for the already holy.
A school, a place where people come because they don't know yet. Then comes the hope that gives this day its line.
In setting it up, he hopes to lay down nothing harsh, nothing heavy. He's honest, though: some things may feel a little strict, for good reasons, to correct faults and to protect love.
When that happens, he asks the beginner not to run away in fear, because the way in is narrow at the start. Then a promise.
As someone goes on in this life and in faith, the heart grows wider, and they run the way of God's commandments with a sweetness of love that's hard to put into words.

teach.h: WHEN THOU DIDST ENLARGE MY HEART.
teach.b: That's the Rule borrowing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart." Look at the shape of it. Narrow at the start, wider as you go.
Strict in places, but never meant to crush. Benedict isn't writing for heroes; he's writing for people who will stall at the light.
And at the very end of the Rule, he'll call the whole book, not just the first chapter, a little rule for beginners. In Benedict's school, nobody graduates.

how: Benedictine communities welcome newcomers through a period of trial and learning, and Benedictines describe their whole life as a school of the Lord's service.

the training year before a monk takes his vows

games.q: you're a new monk. the first weeks feel strict, and you want to leave. what does Benedict tell you?
o: leave: this life isn't for you.
don't run away in fear; the way in is narrow at the start.
work harder until it stops hurting.
games.why: he asks the beginner not to flee, and promises that as you go on, the heart grows wider.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're new at, or keep starting over: prayer, a language, a new job, being a parent, and notice how the voice in your head talks to you about it.
Now try Benedict's tone instead, strict where it matters, nothing harsh, nothing heavy, and say quietly: I'm learning. If you pray, ask God to widen your heart a little at a time.

wordCard.voice: A school for beginners. Benedict's picture of the monastery: a school of the Lord's service, where he hopes to set down nothing harsh or heavy, and where the heart grows wider as you go. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Rule's Prologue: a school of the Lord's service.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing harsh. In Benedict's school, everyone is still a beginner, and that's allowed. Until tomorrow.
